title: Language core: exceptions, resources and streams (Java)
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.
description: Checked vs unchecked exceptions, try-with-resources and suppressed exceptions, finally traps, streams (filter, map, flatMap, groupingBy, toMap), lazy evaluation and Optional.
source: Oracle Java Tutorials: exceptions; JLS 14.20.2 (try-finally) and 14.20.3 (try-with-resources); java.util.stream and java.util.Optional docs; Effective Java (Bloch) items 69-77; Baeldung; GeeksforGeeks interview lists

questions.prompt: Write a Java method static String firstLine(Path p) throws IOException that returns the first line of a text file and always closes the reader, using try-with-resources.
questions.starter: static String firstLine(Path p) throws IOException {

checks.label: opens a reader/scanner on the path
reads a line and returns it

questions.explanation: Resources declared in the parentheses must implement AutoCloseable and are closed automatically, even on exceptions. Files.lines(p) in a try-with-resources is equally valid.

The return value is evaluated and saved before finally runs, so reassigning the local x in finally cannot change it. (A return inside finally would override it and also swallow exceptions, which is why it is a code smell.) Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In try-with-resources, resources are closed in the reverse order of their declaration.
questions.reason: A resource used in try-with-resources must implement AutoCloseable.

whys.a: R is true but it does not explain the ordering; the reverse order exists because later resources may depend on earlier ones.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true, but the AutoCloseable requirement is unrelated to the closing order.
whys.c: R is true: the compiler rejects other types.
whys.d: A is true: JLS 14.20.3 specifies reverse order.

questions.explanation: Reverse closing mirrors construction, e.g. close the BufferedReader before the FileReader it wraps. Exceptions from close() are added as suppressed exceptions to the primary one.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about Java exceptions.

options.text: If the try body throws A and close() then throws B, A propagates and B is attached via getSuppressed().
options.why: Correct: this is how try-with-resources avoids losing the original failure.

options.text: A custom class that extends RuntimeException is an unchecked exception.
options.why: Correct: the compiler does not force callers to catch or declare it.

options.text: catch (Exception e) also catches OutOfMemoryError.
options.why: OutOfMemoryError is an Error, which is a sibling of Exception under Throwable.

options.text: catch (IOException | Exception e) compiles as a multi-catch.
options.why: It does not: alternatives in a multi-catch must not be subclasses of one another. (Statement is false, so do not select it.)

options.text: A finally block still runs if the try block calls System.exit(0).
options.why: The JVM halts, so finally is skipped.

questions.explanation: Unchecked exceptions signal programming errors; checked exceptions model recoverable conditions the caller must handle. Do not swallow exceptions silently, and wrap with a cause to keep the stack trace.

questions.prompt: Match each Java feature to what it does.

right.text: Declares the checked exceptions a method may let propagate
Closes AutoCloseable resources and records close failures as suppressed
Handles two unrelated exception types in one block
Keeps the original failure available through getCause()
Unchecked: the compiler does not force callers to catch or declare it
Turns a checked exception into an unchecked one automatically

questions.explanation: Each feature has one job; none of them converts exception kinds automatically.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about Java exceptions and resources.
questions.text: A {1} exception must be caught or declared in a throws clause; try-with-resources calls {2} on each resource automatically, and exceptions thrown by close() while another exception is in flight are recorded as {3} exceptions.
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions are enforced by the compiler; suppressed exceptions are read with Throwable.getSuppressed().

questions.prompt: What does Stream.of(1,2,3,4,5,6).filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).map(n -> n * n).reduce(0, Integer::sum) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Even numbers 2, 4, 6 are squared to 4, 16, 36 and summed: 56.

questions.prompt: Given List<String> words, write a Java stream expression that builds Map<Integer, List<String>> byLength grouping the words by their length.
questions.explanation: Add a downstream collector for aggregation, e.g. groupingBy(String::length, Collectors.counting()). A plain loop with computeIfAbsent also works but is not what the stem asks.

questions.prompt: Given Optional<String> name, write one Java expression that returns its value, or "anon" when it is empty.
questions.explanation: orElseGet(() -> "anon") is equally correct and only builds the default when it is needed.

questions.prompt:
What is printed?
Stream.of("a", "b", "c")
  .peek(s -> System.out.print("p" + s + " "))
  .filter(s -> !s.equals("b"))
  .findFirst();
What is the output?

options.text: pa pb pc
options.why: Intermediate operations are lazy and findFirst short-circuits; the pipeline does not touch every element.

options.text: pa only
options.why: Correct: "a" passes the filter and findFirst stops the pipeline at once, so b and c are never visited.

options.text: pa pb
options.why: The first matching element ends the pipeline before b is pulled.

options.text: no output
options.why: findFirst is a terminal operation, so the pipeline runs.

questions.explanation: Streams are pull-based and lazy: nothing happens until a terminal operation, and short-circuiting ops (findFirst, limit, anyMatch) stop early. A stream also cannot be reused: a second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Java method that can throw a checked exception must either catch it or declare it in a throws clause.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is the compiler rule, but RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked, so R is false.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is the compiler rule, but RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked, so R is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is the compiler rule, but RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked, so R is false.
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: A is the compiler rule, but RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked, so R is false.

questions.explanation: Errors and RuntimeException subclasses are unchecked; all other Throwable subclasses are checked.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Optional.get() is the safest way to read a value because it never throws.
questions.reason: Optional.get() throws NoSuchElementException when the Optional is empty.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is false because get() throws on an empty Optional, which R states correctly.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is false because get() throws on an empty Optional, which R states correctly.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: A is false because get() throws on an empty Optional, which R states correctly.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because get() throws on an empty Optional, which R states correctly.

questions.explanation: Prefer orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow or ifPresent to calling get() blindly.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In Java, optional.orElse(expensive()) calls expensive() even when the Optional already holds a value.
questions.reason: Java evaluates method arguments eagerly before the method is invoked.

whys.a: Correct: arguments are evaluated first, so use orElseGet(() -> expensive()) to defer the work.
whys.b: R is the reason for A, not an unrelated fact.

questions.explanation: orElseGet takes a Supplier and runs it only when empty. Also avoid Optional.get() without a check; prefer orElseThrow, map and ifPresent.

options.text: IllegalStateException: stream already operated upon
options.why: Correct: a stream can be consumed once; a terminal operation closes it.

options.text: It prints 3, because count does not consume the stream
options.why: Streams are single-use, so the second terminal call fails.

options.text: It prints 0, because the first count consumed all the data
options.why: Java does not return an empty result; it throws.

options.text: NoSuchElementException, as no element is left to count
options.why: That is thrown by Optional.get or iterators, not by reusing a stream.

questions.explanation: Create a new stream from the source (or use a Supplier<Stream<T>>) for each pipeline.

questions.prompt:
What happens when this Java code runs?

Stream.of("a", "bb", "cc")
  .collect(Collectors.toMap(String::length, s -> s));

What is the result?

options.text: IllegalStateException: Duplicate key 2
options.why: Correct: bb and cc both map to key 2, and the two-argument toMap has no merge function, so it throws.

options.text: It returns {1=a, 2=cc}, the later value wins
options.why: Wrong: that is what a merge function such as (x, y) -> y would do; without one the collector fails.

options.text: It returns {1=a, 2=bb}, the first value wins
options.why: Wrong: toMap does not silently keep the first value; HashMap.put semantics are not used here.

options.text: It returns {1=[a], 2=[bb, cc]}
options.why: Wrong: grouping into lists is the job of Collectors.groupingBy, not toMap.

questions.explanation: Pass a third argument toMap(k, v, (x, y) -> y) to resolve clashes, or use groupingBy. Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: What does Stream.of(List.of(1, 2), List.of(3), List.<Integer>of()).flatMap(List::stream).map(v -> v * 2).filter(v -> v > 2).count() return?
questions.explanation: flatMap flattens the three lists into 1, 2, 3 (the empty list adds nothing); doubling gives 2, 4, 6; only 4 and 6 are greater than 2, so the count is 2. Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: What does Stream.iterate(1, x -> x * 2).limit(5).reduce(0, Integer::sum) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The pipeline is lazy and limit(5) stops the infinite stream: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31.

options.text: Prints 7 and the RuntimeException is discarded
options.why: Correct: a return in finally overrides the pending exception, so it vanishes without a trace.

options.text: Throws RuntimeException: x after finally runs
options.why: Wrong: the abrupt completion of the finally block replaces the try block outcome, so the exception never propagates.

options.text: Does not compile: missing return statement
options.why: Wrong: both paths end abruptly (throw, then return in finally), so the compiler accepts it, usually with a warning.

options.text: Prints 0, the default value of int
options.why: Wrong: nothing is defaulted; the explicit return 7 supplies the result.

questions.explanation: Never return, break or continue inside finally: it swallows exceptions. Verified by running it.
